original.title: The Logic of Scientific Discovery
original.note: Open Library lists this work under its original title 'Logik der Forschung' (1935); 1959 is the English edition cited here. The ISBN belongs to one edition of that work.

core_idea: Reality exists independently of us, but we can know it only imperfectly. Theories can never be proven, only tested and falsified, and observation is always shaped by theory, so claims are warranted conjectures open to revision.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: Testing a hypothesis while admitting measurement error and bias.
Most quantitative and many mixed-methods designs.
Typical designs: experiments and quasi-experiments, surveys, triangulation.
common_mistakes: Writing 'positivism' in the methodology chapter when the position described is post-positivist.
Treating a non-rejected hypothesis as proven.
Ignoring how theory shaped what was measured.

development.adds: Science works within paradigms; observation is theory-laden.
Clear statement of post-positivism for social and educational research.

strands.name: Critical rationalism
strands.summary: Falsification as the criterion of science.

strengths.point: Keeps the goal of objective knowledge while accepting fallibility.
Gives a logic for experimental and quasi-experimental design.

source.title: Quasi-Experimentation: Design & Analysis Issues for Field Settings

critiques.point: No single scientific method exists; methodological rules are regularly and fruitfully broken.
Realities are multiple and constructed, so inquiry cannot be detached from the inquirer.
